subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer about a speaker

items.prompt:
A classmate gives a short speech: 'My family went to the mountains last summer. We hiked on a trail and saw a waterfall. It was the most amazing thing I had ever seen.' 
Which question best gathers MORE information about the speaker's experience?
A) 'Do you like mountains?'
B) 'How high was the waterfall you saw?'
items.answer: B) 'How high was the waterfall you saw?'

steps: Option A asks for a general opinion — not gathering new information.
Option B asks about a specific detail (the waterfall) the speaker mentioned — it collects more information about that experience.

items.prompt: A teacher explains: 'We are going to learn about metamorphosis — the way some animals change their form as they grow.' A student does not understand 'metamorphosis.' Write the question the student should ask.
items.answer: 'Can you explain what metamorphosis means?' or 'What exactly is metamorphosis?'

steps: Metamorphosis is an unfamiliar word the teacher used.
The student should ask directly about the word she does not understand.
This is a vocabulary clarification question connected to the speaker's statement.

items.prompt:
A student presenter says: 'Polar bears are very good swimmers. They can swim for long distances.' A classmate asks: 'How far can they swim?' 
Is this a clarifying question or a question to get more information? Explain.
items.answer: It is a question to get more information. The speaker did not give a specific distance. The classmate wants to know exactly how far — a detail not yet provided.

steps: A clarifying question asks the speaker to re-explain something unclear.
A 'get more info' question asks for a new detail not yet shared.
'How far can they swim?' fits the second type — the speaker said 'long distances' but did not specify.

items.prompt:
A teacher finishes a lesson about plants. She says: 'Plants need sunlight, water, and soil to grow. Without any one of these, the plant will not survive.'
A student asks: 'What happens if a plant has water and soil but no sunlight?' Is this a good follow-up question?
A) Yes — it asks the speaker to explain something more specifically.
B) No — the teacher already answered everything.

steps: The teacher gave general information but did not describe each specific scenario.
This question asks for more specific information — 'what happens if only one condition is missing?'
It shows active listening and a desire to understand the topic more deeply.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Owls are nocturnal, which means they are active at night.' A student thinks she understands but wants to confirm. What question could she ask?
A) 'So nocturnal means active at night?'
B) 'What is your favorite bird?'
items.answer: A) 'So nocturnal means active at night?'

steps: Option A rephrases the definition and asks the speaker to confirm — this checks understanding.
Option B is off-topic.
Checking understanding is a valuable question type (paraphrasing back to the speaker).

items.prompt:
A classmate presents about his hobby: 'I collect coins from different countries. I have coins from 12 countries so far.' After the presentation, a student asks: 'Which country's coin is your favorite?'
Is this a good question? What information does it gather?
items.answer: Yes, it is a good question. It asks the speaker for a personal detail (a favorite) that adds to the audience's understanding of his collection and enthusiasm for the hobby.

steps: The speaker mentioned collecting coins from 12 countries but did not say which was his favorite.
Asking for a favorite invites the speaker to elaborate and share something personal and specific.
This connects to the speaker's topic and gets new information.

items.prompt: A teacher explains an art project. She says: 'You will need to fold the paper three times and then cut along the dotted line.' A student is confused about when to cut. What clarifying question should she ask?
items.answer: 'After which fold should I cut along the dotted line?' or 'Do I cut after all three folds or after just one fold?'

steps: The student is unclear about the sequence (fold THEN cut — but after which fold?).
A clarifying question should identify the specific confusion: 'Do I fold all three times first, then cut?'

items.prompt:
A classmate says: 'I take dance lessons every Tuesday. I am learning a style called hip hop.' A listener asks: 'What is hip hop dance?' Categorize this question:
A) Clarifying question (the listener is confused)
B) Gathering more information (the listener wants to know more about something mentioned)

steps: The listener is not confused by what was said. She wants to know more about hip hop dance.
This is a 'gather more information' question — asking the speaker to elaborate on a detail she mentioned.

items.prompt:
A student gives a show-and-tell about a rock she found. She says: 'I found this rock at the beach. It is very smooth.' A classmate wants to ask a good question. Which is better?
A) 'Why is the rock smooth?'
B) 'Do you like the beach?'

steps: Option A asks the speaker to explain something she mentioned (the smooth rock).
Option B asks for a general opinion not related to the detail she shared about the rock.

items.prompt:
Why is it important to listen carefully before asking a question about a speaker?
A) So you know what the speaker said and can ask a relevant question
B) So you can think of unrelated topics to bring up
items.answer: A) So you know what the speaker said and can ask a relevant question

steps: You can only ask a good, connected question if you listened carefully. Without listening, your question may be off-topic or already answered.

items.prompt:
A visitor speaks about being a veterinarian. She mentions that she helps many kinds of animals. A student asks: 'What is the strangest animal you have ever treated?' 
Is this a question to clarify or to get more information?
items.answer: It is a question to get more information. The visitor did not say which animals she treats — the student is asking for a specific, interesting example.

steps: Nothing in the speaker's statement was unclear.
The student wants a new detail (a specific example of an unusual animal).
This is a gather-more-information question.

items.prompt:
After a classmate presents about a science experiment, you want to ask a question. Which is better?
A) 'What surprised you most about the experiment?'
B) 'I wasn't paying attention — can you start over?'
items.answer: A) 'What surprised you most about the experiment?'

steps: Option A asks the speaker for a specific reaction — it gathers new, meaningful information.
Option B shows the listener was not paying attention — not respectful or productive.
Option A is a higher-quality, engaged question.

items.prompt:
A classmate talks about planting a garden. She mentions: 'The tomatoes needed a lot of water but the cactus barely needed any.' A student asks: 'Why does the cactus need less water?' 
Is this connected to what the speaker said?
A) Yes — it asks for an explanation of a detail the speaker mentioned.
B) No — cacti were not part of the garden.

steps: The speaker directly mentioned the cactus needing little water. Asking WHY follows up on that exact detail — a connected, good question.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'I learned to speak two languages — English and Mandarin.' A student asks: 'How did you learn two languages?' What type of question is this?
A) Clarifying (something was unclear)
B) Gathering information (asking for a new detail not yet given)

steps: The speaker stated she speaks two languages, but did not explain HOW she learned. The question asks for a new piece of information.

items.prompt: After a speaker finishes, a student immediately raises her hand and asks a question that the speaker just answered 30 seconds ago. What should the student have done differently?
items.answer: The student should have listened more carefully. She asked a question that had already been answered, which shows she was not fully paying attention. She should listen to the whole presentation before asking questions.

steps: Asking a question already answered wastes time and shows inattention.
Good listeners wait until the speaker finishes and then ask only questions that have NOT been answered.
Before asking, think: 'Did the speaker already address this?'
